cards.front: A {{c1::community}} is all the populations that live together in one place.
cards.quote: A community is all the populations that live together in one place.
cards.section: Explain: populations, communities and food webs

cards.front: In the chain balsam fir → moose → wolf, the wolf is a {{c1::second-order consumer}}.
cards.back: The moose, which eats plants, is the first-order consumer.
cards.quote: A wolf that eats the moose is a second-order consumer.
cards.section: Explain: populations, communities and food webs

cards.front: On Isle Royale, why can the island feed far fewer wolves than moose?
cards.back: Only part of a moose's energy passes to the wolf that eats it, so each wolf needs many moose over its life.
cards.why: Every animal also gives off some energy as heat, which is lost to the chain.
cards.quote: When a wolf eats a moose, only part of the moose's energy passes to the wolf.
cards.section: Explain: populations, communities and food webs

cards.front: What is a food web?
cards.back: A food web links many food chains, showing who eats whom in a community.
cards.quote: A food web links many food chains.
cards.section: Explain: populations, communities and food webs

cards.front: On a wolf-and-moose island, what usually happens to wolves when there are few moose for each wolf, and what does that do for the moose?
cards.back: Wolves tend to catch moose less often. With too little food, fewer wolves survive and raise pups, so the moose can recover.
cards.quote: When there are few moose for each wolf, wolves tend to catch moose less often.

cards.front: Isle Royale, winter 2019: about 2,060 moose and 15 wolves. Winter 2026: about 524 moose and 37 wolves. About how many times more moose for each wolf were there in 2019 than in 2026?
cards.back: 2,060 ÷ 15 ≈ 137 moose for each wolf. 524 ÷ 37 ≈ 14. 137 ÷ 14 is about 10, so about ten times as many in 2019.
cards.quote: In 2019 there were about ten times as many moose for each wolf as in 2026.

cards.front: Why is moose for each wolf only a rough clue that wolves are going hungry?
cards.back: It is one number for the whole island, not each wolf's share, so by itself it cannot show that wolves are hungry.
cards.quote: moose for each wolf is a rough clue, not a measure of what wolves eat.

cards.front: For which kind of predator and place does the rule "wolves run short of food before the moose run out" fit?
cards.back: A predator that eats mostly one kind of prey, in a place like Isle Royale where neither animal can easily leave or arrive.
cards.quote: The rule fits a predator that eats mostly one kind of prey, in a place like Isle Royale where neither animal can easily leave or arrive.

cards.front: A predator on an island has plenty of other food besides one kind of prey. Will the run-short-of-food rule keep that prey from being eaten down to nothing?
cards.back: Not necessarily. A predator with other food may not go hungry, so it could eat that prey down to nothing.
cards.why: The rule depends on the predator running short of food.
cards.quote: A predator with other food may not go hungry, so it could eat one prey down to nothing.

cards.front: In the simulation of the wolf and moose loop, when does the wolf line peak compared with the moose line, and why do real wolves respond late?
cards.back: In the model, a few years after the moose peak. Real wolves respond late because pups take time to be born and grow up.
cards.quote: Look at the timing: the wolf line peaks a few years after the moose line.
cards.section: Explain: how predators and prey change each other's numbers

cards.front: How do herds and packs each help animals get what they need?
cards.back: A herd spots danger and guards the young. A pack hunts large prey, shares it and raises pups.
cards.quote: Pack members share the prey they catch and help care for the pups.

cards.front: Wolves come near a group of muskoxen and near a lone moose. Which animal can form a circle with its young inside, and why not the other?
cards.back: The muskoxen can form the circle, since they live in a herd. Moose mostly live alone, so they do not.
cards.quote: When predators come near, adult muskoxen, large shaggy plant eaters of the far north, can form a circle with their young inside.

cards.front: Packs help wolves hunt and share food. Why does that not remove the limit that food puts on the wolves?
cards.back: A pack can share a kill, but it cannot make more moose. If moose become scarce, wolves usually still run short of food.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that wolves usually run short of food before the moose run out.
cards.quote: A pack can share a kill, but it cannot make more moose.

cards.front: Isle Royale winter counts: 1990 had 15 wolves and about 1,216 moose; 2024 had 30 wolves and about 840 moose. About how many moose for each wolf in each year, and which year had more?
cards.back: 1990: 1,216 ÷ 15 ≈ 81. 2024: 840 ÷ 30 = 28. There were more moose for each wolf in 1990.
cards.quote: About how many moose were there for each wolf in 1990? In 2024? In which year were there more?
cards.section: Elaborate: read the Isle Royale counts

cards.front: From 1980 to 2026 on Isle Royale, how close did the moose come to zero, and what does that show about wolves?
cards.back: The moose rose and fell many times but never came close to zero. The wolves never ate every last moose.
cards.quote: On Isle Royale the moose rose and fell many times from 1980 to 2026, yet never came close to zero.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the Isle Royale counts

cards.front: Isle Royale, winter 1997: about 500 moose and 24 wolves. About how many moose for each wolf? In 1998 there were 14 wolves. Does that fit the rule?
cards.back: 500 ÷ 24 ≈ 21 moose for each wolf, which is few. Wolves fell from 24 to 14 by the next count, which fits the rule.
cards.quote: On the graph, find another winter, not 1997, with few moose for each wolf.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the Isle Royale counts

cards.front: In 1980 there were only about 13 moose for each wolf, and the wolves then crashed from 50 to 14. Why is that not clean evidence for the rule?
cards.back: A dog disease, canine parvovirus, spread among the wolves then, so the crash may not be about food.
cards.why: A second cause was changing the wolf numbers.
cards.quote: In the early 1980s, a dog disease called canine parvovirus spread among the wolves, and their numbers crashed from 50 to 14 in about two years.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the Isle Royale counts

cards.front: Wolves rose from 15 in 2019 to 37 in 2026 while moose fell, even though moose for each wolf got low. Does that break the rule?
cards.back: Not necessarily. People brought 19 new wolves in 2018 and 2019, and the rise after 2018 comes from them and their pups. The rule says wolves could level off or fall later.
cards.quote: In 2018 and 2019, the Park Service brought 19 new wolves to the island; the rise in wolves after 2018 comes from them and their pups.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the Isle Royale counts

cards.front: Design a fair model test of whether prey in a tight group lose fewer members than prey spread out, using 30 paper squares and a cardboard square dropped from above. Name the independent and dependent variables.
cards.back: Independent: how the prey are placed, in one tight group or spread out. Dependent: the number of prey eaten, one per drop that touches any prey. Keep constant: 30 prey, same field, card and drop height, random drop spots. Use 50 drops per setup.
cards.quote: Does living in a group protect prey? Test it with a model.

cards.front: In the paper-square model, the card drops at random spots and eats only one prey per drop. Which loses fewer prey: a tight group or spread-out prey?
cards.back: The tight group loses fewer. It is hit on far fewer drops, and each hit eats only one prey.
cards.quote: If drops land at random all over the field, a tight group is hit on far fewer drops.

cards.front: In the paper-square model, remove the rule that a drop eats only one prey. How does the result for a tight group change?
cards.back: One drop can catch many grouped prey, so the group can lose about as many in all. The group's advantage came from the one-prey rule.
cards.quote: Without that rule, one drop can catch many grouped prey, and the group can lose about as many in all.

cards.front: What can a study of wolf and moose records show, and what can it not show by itself?
cards.back: It can show which factors go with the changes, but it cannot by itself prove a cause.
cards.quote: A study of records like this can show which factors go with the changes, but it cannot by itself prove a cause.

cards.front: Ospreys dive for menhaden in the Chesapeake Bay. Before using the wolf and moose rule on them, what should you ask first?
cards.back: Ask whether the predator eats mostly one kind of prey, in a place where neither animal can easily leave or arrive. The rule fits that kind of predator and place.
cards.quote: Ask first whether the predator eats mostly one kind of prey.
